thread.title: Apple: It's The Process, Not The Outcome - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)

author: Taylor Dart
title: Apple: It's The Process, Not The Outcome - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)
text:
In February of this year, I wrote "Apple: Time For Me To Pack My Bags" and received a lot of flak for my decision. The stock had broken beneath its 40-week moving average while the Nasdaq ( QQQ ) had not, and was the worst performer among the mega caps I was holding. This divergence prompted me to exit my position for a 50%+ gain, and the stock is now sitting 15% higher. While there is absolutely no disputing this was an expensive decision in hindsight, it was the right decision at the time. There is absolutely no point in having a system if you're not going to follow it, and this is why I did not hesitate to follow my system and sell Apple ( AAPL ) when the sell signal occurred. The stock is currently bullish across all time-frames, and I am happy for those that continue to hold it. The goal of this article is to point out that it is the process in trading that is the most important, not the outcome that is known only after the fact.
(Source: TC2000.com)
(Source: TC2000.com)
Taking a look at the weekly chart of Apple below, one would be puzzled at the reason for selling the stock 15% lower at near $160.00 per share. The stock is trading 4% from all-time highs, has broken out of a multi-month base, and is armed with a massive buy-back program. The issue is that everything looks simple and obvious when looking back at a chart after the fact. The way the chart looked at the time I sold it was a different story. The stock was one of the weakest mega-cap tech names while others were barely budging, and the stock had closed below its 40-week moving average for the first time in over a year. Occurrences like these over the past twenty years for Apple have either been non-events or complete busts, and it's impossible to know at the time. Through back-testing my 40-week strategy over a 30-year period going back to the early 80s, I've found closes below 40-week moving averages in up-trends to lead to trend changes or consolidations more often than not. Due to the fact I want to be in stocks that are trending higher, neither consolidations nor broken-up trends are something I want to be involved with.
The most likely rebuttal I'll get to this statement is "Yes, but it's Apple. You can't trade a great company like this like you would other stocks." It is worth noting that this strategy has worked great for Apple in the past, and it has also worked for the old market leaders like Qualcomm ( QCOM ), and new market leaders like Netflix ( NFLX ). I have shown one example of Apple's 40-week sell violations below from the 80s, but there are many more for those willing to do some digging. In 2012, Apple broke below its 40-week moving average and was dead money for nearly two years while the market ( SPY ) itself rose almost 30% in value and stocks like Amazon ( AMZN ) gained over 100%. The year 2000's 40-week violation on Apple saw a more substantial draw-down of 75%.
(Source: TC2000.com)
As we can see in the below examples of Qualcomm, the stock lost 50% or more of its value in a short period after previous 40-week moving average violations. As long as you were willing to repurchase the stock on new setups, this strategy allowed you to capture the majority of the uptrend and not suffer the large draw-downs in between them.
(Source: TradingView.Com)
(Source: TradingView.Com)
In the below examples of Netflix, the stock lost between 60% and 80% of its value on two occasions after breaking its 40-week moving average after strong uptrends. During the one time where the stock did not see a violent decline after breaking its 40-week moving average, it did spend nearly 2.5 years going sideways.
(Source: TradingView.com)
(Source: TradingView.com)
(Source: TradingView.Com)
Looking at the most recent buy signal on Netflix which I took at $98.00, the stock has gained over 400% since. A simple 40-week moving average strategy would have kept you in the stock for this whole move. I have been re-balancing my position along the way as it's such a large winner, and am now down to 1/2 of my initial position bought at $98.00. I sold another 1/8 of my initial position bought at $98.00 at $417.90 this morning for a 425% gain.
(Source: TC2000.com)
So what does any of this have to do with Apple?
The point of this article is to point out one of the most significant issues with some traders I've spoken to. Many traders are Monday Morning Quarterbacks that evaluate their decisions as good or bad only in hindsight. If a stock goes up after they sold it, it was the wrong decision. If a stock goes down and they held it, it was a wrong decision. There is zero way ever to have any consistency in one's trading if you evaluate your trades based on the outcome and not the process. To better illustrate this point, let's turn it into a real-life example.
Let's say you've just finished school and have been looking for a job without any luck for a year. You've sent out hundreds of resumes, have been to fifty or more interviews, and can't seem to catch a break. One morning you sleep in so you don't have time to shower or iron your clothes, sprint out the door without eating breakfast, don't review any notes, and are ten minutes late for the interview. This is the interview where you are the least prepared and the least presentable, but by some stroke of luck, you get the job.
(Source: Jupiter Images)
A person who evaluates things on the outcome and not the process would surmise that this is the new way to approach interviews. Forget showering and preparing the night before, forget eating breakfast, and aim to be a little late. If someone told us this was their plan we would laugh and think it was ridiculous. It would make absolutely zero sense for someone to assume that due to one outcome a process is correct, especially if it goes against all conventional wisdom.
Despite how crazy this would be to come to this conclusion in the real world, traders do this every day when trading. They sell XYZ stock because it closes below its 200-day moving average on massive volume, but it bounces 10% the next day. Due to the outcome of it shaking them out and rallying against them, they now change their rules to not sell on 200-day moving average violations, or even worse, they now buy on 200-day moving average breakdowns. This is a flawed strategy and one that has proven to be inferior to being long above the 200-day moving average and playing defense when it breaks, but one outcome that's been magnified has now changed the trader's process. How can a trader ever hope to have a consistent and profitable system when they are trading purely out of hindsight? Just as you would not change all of your daily habits based on one single outcome in the real world, you should not do this in trading. Living out of hindsight and trading out of retrospect are poisonous to one's process and accomplish nothing in the long run. All they do is lead to style drift and no real plan.
Since I operate from a rigid approach and am disciplined to it, I had no choice but to sell Apple. Was the decision I made an expensive one and the wrong decision in hindsight? Absolutely. Despite this fact, I would make the same decision next time and not hesitate to sell the stock. The damage from not following one's selling rules and abandoning all discipline is much more significant than the money lost on one single trade by selling early. I believe trading rules to be like following a diet. Each time one breaks their trading rules and has no discipline, the easier it is to continue breaking them. This is the same with a strict diet as the more you "cheat" on your diet, the easier it becomes to keep cheating. I believe traders should be focused on the process of their trades and grade them this way, not based on the outcome.
I am more pleased with myself losing money but trading strictly with my rules than breaking my rules and making money. This is why I find it so comical that there are traders out there that call themselves professionals that have zero discipline and break their rules daily. If you have no discipline in your trading, you are the furthest thing from a professional. Emotional discipline is the one ingredient that is found in nearly all professionals and entrepreneurs, those that don't trade with discipline are just flying by the seat of their pants, and this is not sustainable. The most alarming part about this approach is that it's not measurable. How do you know if the way you are trading is profitable if it can't be measured? If a system is not rigid and you have no discipline to your system, it is not measurable; it's random.
So how does my system currently look for Apple?
(Source: TC2000.com)
Apple is currently trading above a rising 40-week moving average and has broken out of a box just above the $180.00 level. As long as the stock can find support at the top of this box (previous resistance), the stock will remain bullish across the majority of time-frames with momentum to the upside. If I were long the stock currently, I would be staying with the stock as long as it does not close below $170.00 on a weekly basis.
On the daily chart below, we can see that Apple is pulling back near the top of its base and right above its 50-day moving average. Ideally, the bulls are going to want to defend this level. If the stock is going to continue to be a marginal leader, I would rather not see the stock break below its 50-day moving average while the market is well above its 50-day moving average. The stock is currently a little oversold on its lower time-frames, so it will be key to see if the bulls find support from these levels.
(Source: TC2000.com)
From a fundamental perspective, things remain rosy for the stock. The company has initiated a massive buyback program, annual earnings continue to grow at a good pace, and revenue growth actually accelerated last quarter. A look at Annual EPS is below:
2013: $5.68
2014: $6.45
2015: $9.22
2016: $8.31
2017: $9.21
2018: $11.49 (Estimates)
As we can see from the above annual earnings numbers, the trend is clearly up. The stock underwent a brief hiccup in 2016 with its first annual EPS decline since 2013, but has since seen EPS recover nicely and make a new high above the 2015 high of $9.22. Estimates for 2018 remain strong with roughly 25% annual EPS growth slated for 2018. This is even more impressive from a company of Apple's size as often mega-caps lack innovation and see earnings growth taper off in the single digit range annually.
From a sales standpoint, revenue growth also remains strong. The three quarters preceding the most recent quarter saw revenue growth of 7%, 12%, and 13% year over year. The most recent quarter came in at 16% revenue growth and has moved back into the upper teens. It is always a good sign when record earnings are supported by an acceleration in revenue growth. Finally, the company's return on equity is incredible for a company of its size. Apple has one of the strongest return on equity rates of most mega-cap tech names at 37%. This figure dwarfs most of its peers.
Based on the above fundamentals, the company still remains a growth stock despite its gargantuan market cap. There are currently no signs of this slowing down based on 2018 and 2019 estimates. The company's bullish technical picture is supported by strong fundamental as the company is expecting yet another new all-time high in EPS for both 2018 and 2019.
As mentioned in my Apple article in February, I have stayed long Netflix from my $98.00 purchase, as well as Mastercard ( MA ) and Google ( GOOG ) (NASDAQ: GOOGL ). These stocks are all up more than Apple year-to-date, they all held up better than Apple, and they are the real leaders. Netflix is up 118% year-to-date, Mastercard is up 34%, and Google is up nearly 13%. As can be seen in the chart of all four stocks below, the only stock that broke its 200-day moving average on a daily closing basis during the February correction was Apple. Not surprisingly, it is also the laggard of the group and up the least year-to-date. Does this mean it's a bad stock and shouldn't be held? No. My goal when trading, however, aligns with a quote by Richard Driehaus from Market Wizards written by Jack Schwager.
(Source: Market Wizards by Jack Schwager)
(Source: TC2000.com)
In summary, I believe Apple to be a hold currently, but unfortunately I am not long the stock. Most importantly, this growth comes at a reasonable price. I continue to stalk the chart for a potential entry and may consider adding back my position if it can set something up in the next couple weeks as it tries to build a new base above its recent multi-month box breakout. There is no question I regret selling Apple from an outcome standpoint below $160.00 in February. Do I care about missing some gains in the stock? No. I operate on a strict process and don't look back in hindsight and torture myself with single outcomes. My systems are designed based on the next thousand trades, not the one or two trades that shook me out last week. I want to be long the leaders and Apple is no longer a leader. Stocks like ServiceNow ( NOW ), Netflix, Amazon, Fair Isaac ( FICO ) are clear leaders in this market as they have been outpacing the market's gains exponentially this year, and barely pausing for more than a few days. Apple is a great stock with a great dividend that is a hold, but it's not the fastest horse in this race anymore. As long as the stock remains above $170.00 on a weekly closing basis, it remains bullish across most time-frames and the new range looks to be $170.00-210.00.
Disclosure: I am/we are long NFLX, AMZN, NOW, FICO, UPRO, MA, GOOG.
Additional disclosure: I would love to know what companies you believe are superior long ideas that are underrated. While I do track 3000+ stocks on a weekly basis, there are always a few that fly under my radar. My articles get plenty of comments, and I'm always open to new ideas and food for thought.
